questions.q: What percentage of CO₂ is transported as bicarbonate in human blood, and which enzyme catalyses its formation inside erythrocytes?
questions.a: 70% of CO₂ is transported as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), catalysed by carbonic anhydrase inside erythrocytes. A wrong answer (e.g., "20-25% as bicarbonate" or "carbonic anhydrase in plasma") reveals confusion between the three transport modes and mislocalisation of the enzyme — students often forget that carbonic anhydrase is concentrated in RBCs, not plasma, and that bicarbonate is the dominant form, not carbamino-haemoglobin.

questions.q: Explain why CO₂ binds to haemoglobin more readily at tissues than at alveoli, even though the binding site is the same.
questions.a: At tissues, high pCO₂ and low pO₂ favour carbamino-haemoglobin formation (Haldane effect); at alveoli, low pCO₂ and high pO₂ cause dissociation. A wrong answer focusing only on pCO₂ ("high pCO₂ at tissues drives binding") misses the critical role of pO₂ — the Haldane effect means deoxygenated haemoglobin has higher affinity for CO₂ than oxygenated haemoglobin. Students who omit pO₂'s influence cannot explain why CO₂ unloads efficiently at the lungs despite a modest pCO₂ gradient.

questions.q: A person hyperventilates before a breath-hold dive. Predict how this affects CO₂ transport and the urge to breathe, referencing the bicarbonate equilibrium.
questions.a: Hyperventilation blows off CO₂, lowering blood pCO₂ and shifting the equilibrium CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ leftward, reducing [H⁺] (respiratory alkalosis). This delays the chemoreceptor-triggered urge to breathe (which responds to H⁺/CO₂), but does not increase O₂ stores. A wrong answer ("hyperventilation increases O₂ so you can hold breath longer") reveals the classic misconception that the breath-hold limit is set by O₂ lack rather than CO₂/H⁺ buildup — students confuse the driver of respiratory drive.

questions.q: Compare the direction of the chloride shift at tissues versus alveoli, and explain how it maintains electroneutrality during CO₂ transport.
questions.a: At tissues: HCO₃⁻ exits RBC → Cl⁻ enters (Hamburger phenomenon); at alveoli: HCO₃⁻ enters RBC → Cl⁻ exits. This counter-transport maintains electroneutrality as HCO₃⁻ moves down its concentration gradient. A wrong answer (e.g., "Cl⁻ moves with HCO₃⁻ in same direction") shows failure to grasp that anion exchange (Band 3 protein) is a strict 1:1 swap — students often memorise "chloride shift" as a phrase without understanding it solves the charge imbalance created by HCO₃⁻ efflux.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Since CO₂ is more soluble than O₂, it diffuses faster across the alveolar membrane, so CO₂ transport in blood is less dependent on chemical conversion than O₂ transport."
questions.a: The statement is false. While CO₂ solubility is 20-25× higher, enabling rapid diffusion, 93% of CO₂ transport still requires chemical conversion (bicarbonate + carbamino) — only 7% dissolves physically. O₂ transport is 97% chemical (oxyhaemoglobin). A wrong evaluation ("true because solubility helps diffusion") conflates membrane diffusion rate with blood transport capacity — students confuse the physical diffusion step (where solubility matters) with the carriage step (where chemical binding dominates for both gases).

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a pH indicator and exhaled air to demonstrate the CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻ equilibrium shift, and explain what colour change you would observe when blowing into the solution versus when a plant photosynthesises in it.
questions.a: Use phenol red (red at pH 7.4, yellow below pH 6.8). Blowing exhaled air (high pCO₂) into water shifts equilibrium right → H⁺ increases → solution turns yellow. Placing a photosynthesising plant (e.g., Hydrilla) in it consumes CO₂, shifting equilibrium left → H⁺ decreases → solution turns red. A poor answer (e.g., "colour changes but cannot explain direction") reveals inability to link Le Chatelier's principle to the carbonic acid equilibrium — students treat the reaction as one-way rather than a reversible buffer system.
